title: Sum of Subarray Minimums
description: Brute force to optimized: enumerating every subarray directly versus the monotonic stack contribution technique that counts each element's dominance.

blocks.text: Given an array of integers arr, find the sum of min(b) over every (contiguous) subarray b of arr. Since the answer may be very large, return it modulo 10^9 + 7.

blocks.caption: The monotonic stack contribution technique finds, for each element, exactly how many subarrays it is the minimum of, without ever enumerating those subarrays directly

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Sum of MIN over every subarray\"","The classic monotonic stack \"contribution technique\": for each element, count exactly how many subarrays it is the minimum of"],["Each element's contribution to the total is its value times the COUNT of subarrays it dominates","That count factors into independent left-boundary and right-boundary choices, each found via a monotonic stack pass"]]}

blocks.text: Rather than computing every subarray's minimum directly and summing them, the total can be reframed per ELEMENT: how much does each individual value in arr contribute to the grand total, across every subarray where it happens to be the minimum? Summing each element's value times how many such subarrays it is the minimum of gives the same final answer.

blocks.title: Analogy: Tallying How Often Each Team Member Is the "Weakest Link"
blocks.text: Imagine every possible contiguous GROUP of team members lined up, and wanting to sum up "the weakest member's skill level" across every such group. Instead of forming every group and checking who is weakest each time, it is equivalent (and far more efficient) to ask, for EACH person individually, "in how many groups am I specifically the weakest one?" and sum up their skill level times that count.

blocks.caption: For each element, its previous strictly-smaller neighbor and next smaller-or-equal neighbor bound exactly which subarrays it is guaranteed to be the minimum of

blocks.text: Before computing every subarray's minimum by directly tracking a running minimum as each subarray extends (O(n^2)), notice the total sum can be reframed per-element: how many subarrays is EACH element the minimum of, computed directly via monotonic stack boundaries.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For arr[i] to be the minimum of some subarray, that subarray's left edge must fall strictly AFTER the nearest smaller element to the left (otherwise that smaller element would be included, becoming the TRUE minimum instead), and its right edge must fall at or before the nearest value <= arr[i] to the right.

Observation 2: The number of valid LEFT edges is (i - prevLess[i]), and the number of valid RIGHT edges is (nextLessOrEqual[i] - i); since these choices are INDEPENDENT, the total number of subarrays where arr[i] is the minimum is their PRODUCT.

Observation 3: Both prevLess and nextLessOrEqual are computed via the standard monotonic stack "next smaller element" technique, just tracking BOUNDARY INDICES rather than resolving direct matches.

Observation 4: Using STRICT inequality on the left search and NON-STRICT (<=) on the right search is essential to avoid double-counting when duplicate values are present in the array.

This is the monotonic stack "contribution technique": for each element, count exactly how many subarrays it is the minimum of (via independent left and right boundary counts), multiply by its value, and sum across all elements.
Directly enumerate every subarray, tracking the running minimum as it extends, and sum up each subarray's minimum as it is formed.

items: For each starting index i, extend the subarray one element at a time (index j from i to n-1), updating the running minimum.
Add the current subarray's minimum to a running total at every extension.

codes.python:
MOD = 10**9 + 7

def sum_subarray_mins(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        min_val = arr[i]
        for j in range(i, n):                                              # extend the subarray one element at a time
            min_val = min(min_val, arr[j])                                 # track the running minimum as the subarray grows
            total = (total + min_val) % MOD
    return total


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(sum_subarray_mins([3, 1, 2, 4]))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Extending the subarray one element at a time lets the running minimum be tracked incrementally, avoiding a full rescan for every subarray.
The modulo is applied at each addition step to keep the running total from growing unboundedly large.

blocks.text: Correctly sums every subarray's minimum, since it directly and completely enumerates every possible (start, end) pair.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2), enumerating all O(n^2) subarrays.
Space: O(1) extra.
Limitation: O(n^2) does not scale to the problem's constraints (up to 3*10^4 elements); the monotonic stack contribution technique computes the same total in O(n).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force enumerates every subarray explicitly. Instead, for each element, compute how many subarrays it is the MINIMUM of, using two monotonic stack passes: one finding each element's nearest strictly-smaller left neighbor, one finding its nearest smaller-or-equal right neighbor. Multiply the resulting left-choice-count by right-choice-count, multiply by the element's own value, and sum across all elements.

Compute prevLess[i] via a forward monotonic stack pass (popping while the stack's top is >= arr[i]). Compute nextLessEq[i] via a backward monotonic stack pass (popping while arr[i] is strictly less than the stack's top, so ties remain, giving the <= boundary). Each element's contribution is arr[i] * (i - prevLess[i]) * (nextLessEq[i] - i); sum these (mod 10^9+7).
Compute each element's "minimum of how many subarrays" count via two monotonic stack passes, then sum its weighted contribution.

codes.python:
MOD = 10**9 + 7

def sum_subarray_mins(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    prev_less = [-1] * n                                                    # nearest index to the left with a STRICTLY smaller value
    next_less_eq = [n] * n                                                  # nearest index to the right with a value <= arr[i]

    stack = []
    for i in range(n):
        while stack and arr[stack[-1]] >= arr[i]:                          # pop everything NOT strictly smaller than arr[i]
            stack.pop()
        prev_less[i] = stack[-1] if stack else -1
        stack.append(i)

    stack = []
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        while stack and arr[i] < arr[stack[-1]]:                           # pop everything STRICTLY bigger than arr[i] (ties stay, giving <=)
            stack.pop()
        next_less_eq[i] = stack[-1] if stack else n
        stack.append(i)

    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        left = i - prev_less[i]                                            # choices for the subarray's LEFT edge
        right = next_less_eq[i] - i                                        # choices for the subarray's RIGHT edge
        total = (total + arr[i] * left * right) % MOD                     # arr[i] is the minimum in exactly left*right subarrays
    return total


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(sum_subarray_mins([3, 1, 2, 4]))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), two linear monotonic stack passes.
Space: O(n), for the stacks and boundary arrays.

For arr[i] to be the minimum of a subarray, every element within that subarray must be >= arr[i], and the boundaries of the LARGEST such subarray are exactly determined by where a smaller (or, on one side, smaller-or-equal) value appears. Since the left-edge choice and right-edge choice are entirely independent (any valid left edge can pair with any valid right edge), multiplying their counts gives the exact total number of subarrays where arr[i] is the minimum, directly usable as a multiplier for its contribution.

items: The modulo operation is applied after each addition to the running total, preventing overflow while accumulating potentially many large contributions.
Using a wider integer type (long/long long) for intermediate products (arr[i] * left * right) avoids overflow before the modulo is applied.
The two monotonic stack passes are structurally identical to the standard "next smaller element" technique, just repurposed to find BOUNDARY indices rather than resolve direct value matches.

blocks.text: "Sum of X over all subarrays," where X is an extreme value (min or max), is the defining signal for the monotonic stack contribution technique: reframe the sum per-ELEMENT (how many subarrays is this element the extreme of?) rather than per-SUBARRAY.

items: Using the SAME tie-breaking rule on both sides (both strict or both non-strict), which double-counts (or under-counts) subarrays containing duplicate values.
Forgetting the modulo operation, or applying it inconsistently, risking overflow or an incorrect final answer.
Confusing this problem with Sum of Subarray Ranges (which needs BOTH sum of minimums AND sum of maximums, subtracted); this problem only needs the minimum half.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["A single-element array","The only subarray's minimum is that element itself, so the answer is just that value"],["All elements equal","Every subarray's minimum is that same value; the contribution technique still correctly sums n*(n+1)/2 copies of it"],["Strictly increasing array","Every subarray's minimum is simply its FIRST element, correctly reflected in each element's boundary counts"]]}

items: Explicitly stating "reframe per-element: how many subarrays is THIS specific value the minimum of?" up front demonstrates the key insight that separates this from a naive enumeration approach.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Sum of [min/max] over ALL subarrays" points directly to the monotonic stack contribution technique: count, for each element, how many subarrays it is the extreme of.

items: How does this problem relate to Sum of Subarray Ranges elsewhere in this category? Sum of Subarray Ranges computes exactly this SAME sum of minimums, plus its mirror-image sum of maximums, then subtracts them.

Why is the asymmetric tie-breaking (strict on one side, non-strict on the other) necessary? Without it, a subarray containing multiple copies of the minimum value could have MULTIPLE elements each independently claiming to be "the minimum," inflating the total count.

How would you adapt this to find the sum of subarray PRODUCTS of the minimum, rather than just the sum? A similar contribution technique could work, though products (rather than sums) generally require different aggregation strategies, since contributions do not combine additively in the same simple way.
The foundational half of Sum of Subarray Ranges elsewhere in this category, which combines this exact technique with its mirror-image "sum of subarray maximums."

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (monotonic stack contribution technique): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Monotonic stack contribution technique

Core Idea: For each element, count exactly how many subarrays it is the minimum of, using previous-strictly-smaller and next-smaller-or-equal boundaries (found via monotonic stacks), then sum each element's value times that count
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Reframing "sum over subarrays" as "sum over elements, weighted by how many subarrays each dominates" avoids ever enumerating subarrays directly
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: contribution = arr[i] * (i - prevLess[i]) * (nextLessEq[i] - i), summed (mod 10^9+7)
